把這段部落格文章翻成台灣正體中文：

When we started the project in 2021, we chose SQLite because it was simple and required no separate server. For the first year, this decision worked well. However, as the number of users grew, we began to notice that write operations were becoming a bottleneck. SQLite allows only one writer at a time, which means that when several users tried to save their changes simultaneously, some of them had to wait. At the same time, the database file had grown to more than 10 GB, and backing it up took longer each week. After several discussions, we decided to migrate to PostgreSQL. The migration itself took two months, mainly because we had to rewrite a number of queries that relied on SQLite-specific behavior. Looking back, we do not regret starting with SQLite, but we wish we had planned the migration earlier.

Before you can push code to the server, you need to set up an SSH key. If you already have one, you can skip this step. To generate a new key, open a terminal and run ssh-keygen -t ed25519. The command will ask you where to save the key; pressing Enter accepts the default location in ~/.ssh. You will then be prompted for a passphrase. Although a passphrase is optional, it is strongly recommended, because it protects your key in case your computer is lost or stolen. Once the key has been created, copy the contents of the public key file and paste it into the SSH Keys section of your account settings.
